The repair shop opened between a bakery and a place that sold very expensive lamps.

Its sign read: **SMALL THINGS PUT RIGHT.**

People brought what you would expect: watches, cracked bowls, a radio that could receive only weather reports from a town nobody could find.

The woman behind the counter repaired most of them.

Then someone brought an apology.

It was folded into a coat pocket, where it had been sitting for eleven years.

“I don’t know if it still works,” the customer said.

The woman unfolded it carefully.

“Who’s it for?”

“My brother.”

“And what’s wrong with it?”

He pointed to the middle. “That part where I explain why I did it.”

She read it twice, then drew a line through three sentences.

“Try it now.”

After that, word spread.

People arrived carrying afternoons they had wasted, promises that rattled when shaken, friendships with one side worn thin. A young father brought in his patience, wrapped in a dish towel.

“It used to last all day,” he said.

The woman examined it under a lamp.

“You’ve been using it without sleep.”

“Can you fix it?”

“I can watch the baby for twenty minutes. There’s a chair in the back.”

Not everything could be repaired. She kept no shelf of miracles. Sometimes she handed an object back and said, “You’ll have to learn to live with this.” People generally disliked that, though a few returned years later to say she had been right.

One winter evening, after the bakery had closed and the lamp shop had gone dark, a little girl came in carrying nothing.

“What needs fixing?” the woman asked.

“My mother says the world is broken.”

The woman set down her tools. Through the window she could see the baker struggling with a sack of flour he had forgotten to bring inside.

“Did your mother say which part?”

“No.”

“All right.” She stood and put on her coat. “Let’s start across the street.”
